_note: Flight School v4 (docs/LEARNING_DESIGN.md §11): 6 core lessons, the check ride, and 2 explorer lessons unlocked after missions (`track`, `unlock_after_missions`), then Field School (track `field`: 4 geology lessons that open after the check ride, docs/LEARNING_DESIGN.md §12), in map order (each lesson's `place` is its Moon-map pin). Authored in tools/build_course.py. Every fact cites a {title,url} and names the repo data file(s) it comes from (`from`, relative to backend/data); tests check every number in a fact appears in those files (or is recomputed, for `calc`). Steps accept voice or taps; app/academy/grade.py lists the accept types. A `video` step (app/academy/content.py VIDEO_MEDIA) is predict -> watch -> reveal and never blocks; a lesson's optional `prep` is a hands-on Mission prep task with its NASA activity source.

lessons.title: Know your Moon
lessons.brief: Let's explore the Moon, from its big dark plains to the south pole.

facts.text: Artemis II flew its crew around the Moon in April 2026. NASA plans the first south-pole landing for Artemis IV, in early 2028.
NASA's 2024 list of 9 possible landing regions near the south pole includes Malapert Massif and de Gerlache Rim 2.

source.title: NASA Provides Update on Artemis III Moon Landing Regions (Oct 2024)

facts.text: The Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same side always faces us.
Shackleton is a crater about 21 km wide and about 4 km deep. The south pole is on its edge.

facts.text: Craters that never see the Sun are some of the coldest spots measured: below -246 C.

source.title: NASA Science: Weather on the Moon

lessons.title: Phases and eclipses
lessons.brief: The Moon seems to change shape. Let's find out why, then catch an eclipse.

facts.text: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As it goes around Earth, we see more or less of that half.
Sunrise to sunrise on the Moon takes about 29.5 Earth days, so the phases repeat about every month.
In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow covers the Moon. It can look reddish.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is an eclipse?

facts.text: Behind the Moon, the Artemis II crew watched the Moon cover the Sun, with the Sun's glowing corona around it.

lessons.title: Power from the Sun
lessons.brief: Solar panels need sunlight. Let's see how the Sun moves at the pole.

facts.text: Day and night sweep around the Moon once every 29.5 Earth days.
At the pole the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5 degrees above a flat horizon.
Averaged over a year, Shackleton's rim gets sunlight about 86% of the time and Malapert about 73%.

source.title: Glaser et al. 2018, Illumination conditions at the lunar poles, Planetary and Space Science

facts.text: In our model of April 2026, Malapert was in sunlight 35% of the time.
Its longest dark spell in that window lasted 74 hours, more than 3 days.

lessons.title: Radiation and storms
lessons.brief: The Sun sometimes throws out storms. Let's learn to keep a crew safe.

facts.text: China's Chang'e 4 lander measured 1369 microsieverts a day on the Moon, about 2.6 times the cosmic-ray dose inside the ISS, 523 microsieverts a day.

source.title: Zhang et al. 2020, First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface, Science Advances 6:eaaz1334

facts.text: In May 2024 a real solar particle storm hit space near Earth and the Moon. Earth also got huge auroras.
After a big flare, particles can arrive in tens of minutes to a few hours.
On Orion, a sensor gives up to 1 hour of warning. The crew hides behind packed bags for up to 24 hours.
Game doses are doubled so storms matter in 10 days. The powered shields are pretend tech.

source.title: Outpost Luna radiation data and game assumptions

facts.text: LRO has measured cosmic rays since 2009, with its CRaTER instrument.

source.title: NASA Science: LRO science and data

lessons.title: Moon gravity and dust
lessons.brief: Moon gravity and Moon dust both surprise people. Let's test them.

facts.text: At the end of the last Apollo 15 moonwalk in 1971, Commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather. They hit the ground together.
Gravity on the Moon's surface is 0.165 of Earth's, about one sixth. So 30 kg feels like about 5 kg.
Regolith is the Moon's dusty soil. Its tiny, sharp bits cling to everything.

lessons.title: Lessons from Apollo
lessons.brief: Every mission teaches the next. Follow the crews from Apollo to Artemis.

facts.text: Surveyor 3 sent 6,326 pictures. In 1969 Apollo 12 astronauts walked over and took about 10 kg of parts home, including its TV camera.
John Young and Charlie Duke drove the Apollo 16 rover 26.7 km across the Moon's highlands.
On April 6, 2026, Artemis II reached 252,756 miles from Earth, a new record for human spaceflight. It passed Apollo 13's record of 248,655 miles.

source.title: NASA: Artemis II Flight Day 6 lunar flyby updates

facts.text: Artemis III is a 2027 test flight in Earth orbit. Artemis IV, planned for early 2028, is to land two astronauts near the south pole.
NASA plans its Moon Base, humanity's first lunar outpost, near the lunar South Pole. Outpost Luna is a pretend base.
The Artemis II crew proposed the names Integrity and Carroll for two craters. As of November 2026 the IAU has not approved them.

source.title: USGS/IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature: Moon

lessons.title: Craters and lava
lessons.brief: One astronaut said a crater looked like a volcano. Let's find out what really made it.

facts.text: Impact craters are left when an asteroid, meteoroid or comet hits the Moon.
The spray of broken rock is ejecta. Plumes of ejecta settle back as bright rays.
Tycho is about 85 km wide and 110 million years old: young, for the Moon.
The dark maria are cooled lava that flooded giant impact basins, between 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago.

source.title: NASA Science: What is the Moon made of?

steps.prompt: What made the Moon's round craters?
steps.reveal: Space rocks. A crater is an impact, not a volcano.
steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. Each crater is an old impact.

steps.success: Roger. Tycho's rays are splashed rock: ejecta.

steps.prompt: The dark maria are named seas. What are they really?
steps.hint: They were hot and runny once.
steps.success: Correct. Cooled lava, never water.

steps.hint: Guess first.
steps.success: Right. The basin first, then the lava.

steps.prompt: Tycho's rays lie on top of older ground. Is Tycho young or old?
steps.hint: What's on top came later.
steps.success: Correct. About 110 million years: young!

lessons.title: Moon rocks tell time
lessons.brief: Apollo crews brought rocks home. Each one tells part of the Moon's story.

facts.text: The bright highlands are older crust. The dark maria came later, as lava.

source.title: NASA Science: What is the Moon made of?

facts.text: Sample 60025, an anorthosite, is about 4.4 billion years old: a piece of the Moon's first crust.
Sample 15016, a basalt, is 3.4 billion years old. About half of it is holes left by gas bubbles.
Sample 79115 is a breccia: soil and rock bits glued together by impacts. Apollo 17 broke it off a boulder.
